name: What the Case Manager and Team Decide
title: What the Case Manager and Team Decide
answer: In special education, the IEP team, including parents, decides eligibility, goals, services, and placement, and no AI tool may make those decisions. AI may help by drafting goals or flagging eligibility, but the team must form its own view first and treat AI output as only one input. This matters because these decisions shape a child's education for years and because families have the right to participate fully.

sections.body: This idea sets a boundary around the longest human review section in the book, because special education decisions carry the most weight. Under federal law, the IEP team, including the parents, decides whether a student is eligible for special education, what goals and services the student receives, and where the student is educated. Those choices shape a child's education for years, so no tool may make them. The problem it solves is that a drafted goal or a flagged eligibility could quietly become the decision without real discussion. The team should form its own view first and use AI output only as one input.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not divide this practice by grade band, so the same rule applies across a district's special education process. Figure 12.4 lists what the team and case manager decide alongside what AI may help with, and that list should be part of the district's written human review rule from Chapter 3. Case managers should feel free to set aside any AI suggestion that does not fit the student. The final word always belongs to the people who know the child. Families must be real partners, and the goal is more time for real conversation, not less.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not attach a separate evidence label to this idea, but it says the research on human review applies with full force here. It cites Krugel et al., 2023, for the finding that when a machine makes the first call and a person is supposed to check it, people tend to go along, even with poor decisions. In special education, the text explains, that risk means a drafted goal or a flagged eligibility could become the decision without real discussion. The recommended response is for the team to form its own view first and use AI output only as one input. Figure 12.4 is presented as a list of what the team and case manager decide alongside what AI may help with.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear: no tool may make eligibility, goal, service, or placement decisions, and the final word always belongs to the people who know the child. The team and case manager decide, and case managers should feel free to set aside any AI suggestion that does not fit the student. Families must be real partners in these decisions because they know their child in ways no teacher or tool can, and the law gives them the right to participate fully. A process that uses AI to speed through meetings or present decisions as settled undermines that right. The aim is more time for real conversation, not less.
